front: What was the position of African Americans immediately after the Civil War?
p1: 13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery, freeing 4 million people.
p2: Johnson's lenient Presidential Reconstruction offered no political rights at all.
p3: Black Codes were introduced almost immediately, restricting freedpeople's basic freedoms.

front: What were the early political gains of Reconstruction?
p1: The 15th Amendment (1870) guaranteed voting rights, enforced by Union troops.
p2: Before it existed, 500,000 African Americans had already voted in the 1868 Election.
p3: South Carolina's state government briefly had a majority of Black members.

front: What limited these early political gains?
p1: President Johnson was actively opposed to African American political rights.
p2: Enforcement of the 15th Amendment relied weakly on the presence of Union soldiers.
p3: The 15th Amendment did not grant African American women the vote at all.

front: What were social conditions like for African Americans in 1865?
p1: The Freedmen's Bureau (1865–72) established over 1,000 schools across the South.
p2: BUT by 1870 only around 10% of Black children in the South were enrolled.
p3: Southern states introduced Black Codes as a precursor to later segregation.

front: What violence and prejudice did African Americans face in 1865?
p1: The KKK, founded by Confederate General Nathan Bedford Forrest, used terror to stop voting and education.
p2: The Memphis and New Orleans Riots (both 1866) killed dozens of African Americans.
p3: Media spread myths of 'lazy freedmen' and of Black men as a sexual threat to white women.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans in 1865?
p1: Most freedpeople became sharecroppers, paying rent in crops on the same land as slavery.
p2: '40 acres and a mule' was never delivered, due to Johnson's mass pardons to Southern whites.
p3: The vast majority of freedpeople had no property or land at all.

front: What was the position of African Americans in the labour movement in 1865?
p1: African Americans were generally excluded from white labour unions.
p2: The NLU encouraged Black workers to form separate unions of their own instead.
p3: The CNLU (1869) was formed in response by Isaiah Montgomery, but was short-lived.

front: What did the 14th and 15th Amendments achieve?
p1: 14th Amendment (1868): citizenship and equal protection — Johnson's veto was overruled.
p2: 15th Amendment (1870): banned denial of the vote by race, colour or prior servitude.
p3: Radical Republicans won a supermajority in the 1866 midterm elections to push this through.

front: How did Congress enforce Radical Reconstruction?
p1: Reconstruction Act (1867): divided the South into military-occupied districts.
p2: Removed Black Codes and enforced elections under military occupation.
p3: President Grant supported this, suppressing the KKK with the Enforcement Acts (1870–71).

front: What happened to President Johnson during Reconstruction?
p1: Johnson vetoed the 14th Amendment; Congress overrode his veto.
p2: Congress impeached him in 1869 over his obstruction of Reconstruction.
p3: He survived the vote, but was no longer a real threat to Reconstruction's progress.

front: How did KKK terror undermine Reconstruction?
p1: Colfax Massacre (1873): around 100 killed in Louisiana after contested elections.
p2: Terror was designed to stop African Americans voting, seeking education or asserting rights.
p3: Enforcement Acts suppressed the first KKK, but violence and lynching still continued.

front: Why did federal support for Reconstruction collapse?
p1: Deaths of Radical Republicans Sumner and Stevens removed its most committed advocates.
p2: Panic of 1873 shifted Northern attention onto the economic crisis instead.
p3: Southern states' readmission to Congress diluted the Radical Republican majority.

front: How did the Hayes–Tilden Compromise end Reconstruction?
p1: 1877: federal troops were withdrawn from the South as part of the deal.
p2: 'Redeemer' state governments retook power and began weakening Black rights immediately.
p3: Marked the formal end of Reconstruction, clearing the way for Jim Crow's spread.

front: What was the impact of the Freedmen's Bureau?
p1: Established over 1,000 schools and Howard University (1867), one of the first HBCUs.
p2: Closed in 1872 due to the expense of running the programme.
p3: Educational gains proved short-lived without it, as no infrastructure remained to sustain them.

front: What was the 1875 Civil Rights Act, and why did it fail?
p1: Banned segregation in public accommodations across the whole country.
p2: Had no real enforcement mechanism to make this happen in practice.
p3: Showed federal will was already fading two years before Hayes-Tilden ended Reconstruction.

front: What early economic successes did some African Americans achieve despite 1865's conditions?
p1: Some Black-owned businesses emerged in cities like Washington DC, New York and Chicago.
p2: Concentrated in real estate, beauty salons and restaurants serving Black communities.
p3: Success remained the exception — the vast majority stayed trapped in rural poverty.

front: How many African Americans held political office during Reconstruction?
p1: Over 1,500 African Americans held office during Reconstruction, mostly locally.
p2: 22 were elected to the US Federal Congress.
p3: Blanche K. Bruce served a full 6-year term as senator for Mississippi.

front: How did the Supreme Court undermine Reconstruction legally?
p1: Slaughterhouse Case (1873): ruled civil rights were primarily a state, not federal, issue.
p2: US v Cruickshank (1876): ruled individuals couldn't be prosecuted for racial violence at all.
p3: Together, both rulings gutted the 14th Amendment's power to protect Black Americans.

front: How did Jim Crow spread across the South?
p1: First Jim Crow law introduced on Tennessee railroads (1877).
p2: Spread through the 1880s to schools, churches, parks, restaurants and hospitals.
p3: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) and Cummings v Board (1899) gave it full legal legitimacy.

front: Why and how was voter suppression introduced in the Gilded Age?
p1: The Populist Movement's rise in the 1890s was seen as a political threat by Southern elites.
p2: Literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses spread across the South from 1890.
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) ruled these methods did not violate the 15th Amendment.

front: How effective was voter suppression by 1900?
p1: Mississippi's Black voter registration fell from 90% in 1867 to under 6% by 1892.
p2: In Louisiana, Black voter numbers dropped from 13,000 in 1896 to just 5,000 by 1900.
p3: By 1900, Black voter turnout across the South had fallen below 5%.

front: Case study: what happened during the Wilmington Coup (1898)?
p1: White mobs violently overthrew Wilmington, North Carolina's elected biracial government.
p2: 11 African Americans were killed and hundreds were driven from their homes.
p3: Showed that even legitimate political power could be destroyed by organised violence.

front: What was the impact of lynching in the Gilded Age?
p1: 1,875 lynchings were recorded in the 1890s alone — one African American killed every two days.
p2: Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching in 1900.
p3: Congress defeated over 200 attempts to pass federal anti-lynching legislation.

front: What was the impact of convict leasing?
p1: Southern states exploited the 13th Amendment's loophole allowing forced labour for 'crime'.
p2: Disproportionately targeted African Americans, arrested on trivial or fabricated charges.
p3: Subjected many to brutal working conditions akin to slavery itself.

front: How did Booker T. Washington shape Black education and enterprise?
p1: Atlanta Compromise (1895): accepted segregation in exchange for economic opportunities.
p2: Founded the Tuskegee Institute (1881), training thousands in trades and professions.
p3: Secretly funded lawsuits against disenfranchisement while serving as a trusted adviser to Roosevelt.

front: What were the criticisms of Booker T. Washington?
p1: Du Bois (Harvard's first Black PhD, 1895) and Trotter accused him of conceding too much.
p2: His autocratic control of Black organisations limited the scope of Black leadership.
p3: Niagara Movement (1905): Du Bois's direct alternative, demanding full civil rights immediately.

front: How did Ida B. Wells expose the reality of lynching?
p1: 'Southern Horrors' (1892): documented how frequently Black people were lynched in the South.
p2: Statistical analysis showed most victims were not accused of any violent crime at all.
p3: Despite raising awareness, she was unable to make significant change to lynch law itself.

front: How much political progress did African Americans make in the Gilded Age?
p1: By 1887, 22 African Americans had served in Congress, including Hiram Revels, the first Black senator.
p2: The Populist Movement's rise briefly gave some African Americans local office again.
p3: BUT literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses soon reversed these gains entirely.

front: How much economic progress did African Americans make in the Gilded Age?
p1: By 1900, African Americans owned 15 million acres of land.
p2: 50,000 African American professionals worked as doctors, lawyers and teachers, out of 8 million total.
p3: BUT 90% still lived in the South, mostly as agricultural labourers trapped by sharecropping.

front: How different were African American experiences in the North during the Gilded Age?
p1: Better access to industrial jobs and education grew a small Black middle class.
p2: BUT de facto segregation persisted — Chicago confined 5,000, New York's Harlem 23,000.
p3: White unions were hostile, fearing Black workers as wage competition or strikebreakers.

front: How different were African American experiences in the West during the Gilded Age?
p1: Relative racial indifference let figures like Marshal Bass Reeves and Mary Fields thrive.
p2: All-Black towns like Allensworth, California and Dearfield, Colorado allowed self-governance.
p3: BUT the Exoduster movement (1879) saw 40,000 flee to Kansas, only to face hostility there too.

front: What was the National Negro Business League?
p1: Founded by Washington in 1900 to promote a parallel Black economy.
p2: Grew to 600 chapters across 34 states.
p3: Reflected his broader strategy of economic self-reliance over political confrontation.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the early NAACP?
p1: Sparked partly by the Springfield Race Riot (1908), founded 1909 by Du Bois and Ida B. Wells.
p2: Focused on political pressure and legal litigation rather than direct protest.
p3: US v Guinn (1915): won its first major legal victory, striking down grandfather clauses.

front: How did W.E.B. Du Bois shape early Black intellectual life?
p1: Used The Crisis magazine to promote Black intellectualism and cultural achievement.
p2: Advocated the 'Talented Tenth' — that an educated elite should lead the race forward.
p3: Criticised early NAACP leadership, including himself, for being too middle-class in outlook.

front: How did Marcus Garvey build UNIA into a mass movement?
p1: Founded UNIA's New York branch (1917), reaching 4 million members by the 1920s.
p2: The Negro World newspaper spread his message of pride and unity to 200,000 weekly readers.
p3: Black Star Line (1919): a Black-owned steamship company at the heart of his 'Back to Africa' movement.

front: Why did Marcus Garvey's movement decline?
p1: His meetings with the KKK in 1922 alienated many African Americans and civil rights leaders.
p2: 'Garvey Must Go' campaign gained momentum in response.
p3: Deported to Jamaica in 1927 for mail fraud, ending UNIA as a mass movement.

front: What was the impact of Birth of a Nation on the Ku Klux Klan?
p1: Griffith's 1915 film glorified the KKK and depicted Black men as a threat to white women.
p2: Klan membership surged to 5 million, 15% of the population, by the 1920s.
p3: By 1925, the Klan felt confident enough to burn crosses outside NAACP offices.

front: What was the impact of WWI on African Americans?
p1: 380,000 African Americans served in segregated units, including the Harlem Hellfighters.
p2: Wartime industrial demand sparked the first wave of the Great Migration.
p3: 500,000 moved from the rural South to Northern cities between 1916 and 1919.

front: What happened during Red Summer and the Elaine Massacre (1919)?
p1: Returning white soldiers and industrial competition sparked race riots nationwide.
p2: Worst violence occurred in Chicago as tensions boiled over.
p3: In Arkansas, white mobs killed 200+ Black sharecroppers simply for organising over wages.

front: How did the Great Migration reshape Black communities by the 1920s?
p1: 1.6 million African Americans moved to Northern cities between 1910 and 1930.
p2: Created influential Black urban communities — Harlem and Chicago's South Side.
p3: Opened up industrial jobs unavailable to most African Americans in the South.

front: How did the Harlem Renaissance transform Black culture?
p1: 1920s cultural explosion — figures like Langston Hughes and Louis Armstrong gained recognition.
p2: Harlem's population grew from 50,000 to 200,000 between 1910 and 1930.
p3: BUT even during the Renaissance, Black artists faced exclusion from white cultural institutions.

front: What was the impact of the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921)?
p1: White mob destroyed Greenwood, the prosperous 'Black Wall Street' district of Tulsa.
p2: Officially 36 were killed, though estimates run as high as 300.
p3: Showed that Black economic success could still provoke devastating white backlash.

front: What was President Wilson's personal role in setting back civil rights?
p1: Resegregated the federal government in 1913, reversing earlier integration.
p2: Screened and praised Birth of a Nation at the White House in 1915.
p3: His endorsement helped legitimise the second KKK's national revival.

front: What was the scale of Black education by the Progressive Era?
p1: 5,000 Black schools existed by 1915, founded following Washington's example.
p2: BUT only 34% of Black children attended school, against 62% of white children.
p3: Bethune founded the Daytona school for Black girls (1904), later Bethune-Cookman College.

front: How did Walter White expose the truth behind lynching?
p1: An NAACP leader who posed as a white journalist to investigate lynchings in the 1920s.
p2: Used his findings to lobby Congress for anti-lynching legislation.
p3: BUT none of his campaigns succeeded in getting a federal law passed.

front: What happened during the Scottsboro Boys case (1931)?
p1: Nine Black teenagers falsely accused of rape in Alabama.
p2: Faced coerced confessions and brutal treatment by police.
p3: NAACP fought the case for years, exposing the injustice of Southern courts nationally.

front: How strong was the political position of African Americans by 1932?
p1: 1.6 million had moved North in the Great Migration, opening up urban jobs.
p2: Oscar De Priest (1928) became the first Northern Black congressman since Reconstruction.
p3: BUT only around 10% of Black Northerners were registered voters by 1930.

front: How strong was the economic and social position of African Americans by 1932?
p1: By 1920, 40% of Black men in the North held skilled jobs, against 15% in the South.
p2: BUT unemployment reached 50% nationwide, double the 25% general rate.
p3: 75% of Southern African Americans remained trapped as sharecroppers in poverty.

front: What direct relief did the New Deal provide to African Americans?
p1: FERA gave direct cash relief — 20 to 30% of recipients were African American.
p2: 10% of all major New Deal beneficiaries were Black, matching their share of the population.
p3: By 1935, 30% of Black families were benefiting from relief programmes.

front: How did the WPA and PWA help African Americans?
p1: WPA employed over 1 million African Americans in public works by 1939.
p2: WPA arts programmes established 16 Black theatre groups and taught 250,000+ to read.
p3: PWA funded schools and hospitals, employing over 65,000 African Americans by 1940.

front: How did other New Deal programmes help African Americans?
p1: CCC's Black membership grew from 6% in 1936 to 11% by 1939.
p2: Bethune's National Youth Administration helped 300,000 Black youths gain training and jobs.
p3: Resettlement Administration tried to end sharecropping by promoting Black land ownership.

front: What were the limits of New Deal relief programmes for African Americans?
p1: AAA subsidies went to white landowners, displacing Black sharecroppers instead of helping them.
p2: NRA excluded African Americans from many skilled jobs, paying them lower wages.
p3: Federal housing projects often segregated Black families into substandard developments.

front: Why did the New Deal's legal protections still leave African Americans behind?
p1: Social Security Act (1935) excluded farm and domestic workers, most of them Black.
p2: Fair Labour Standards Act (1938) excluded the same groups from its minimum wage.
p3: The TVA set up all-white towns, excluding African Americans from skilled positions entirely.

front: Was Roosevelt's administration an effective supporter of African American rights?
p1: Secretary Harold Ickes pushed anti-segregation policies within his own department.
p2: William H. Hastie became the first Black federal judge in 1937.
p3: Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the DAR to support Marian Anderson's concert (1939).

front: How limited was Roosevelt's support in practice?
p1: Refused to back anti-lynching legislation, fearing the loss of Southern Democrats.
p2: The Black Cabinet had no real power, kept segregated from the administration's white leadership.
p3: By 1936, three-quarters of African Americans had switched to voting Democrat regardless.

front: What was the impact of Executive Order 8802 (1941)?
p1: Randolph's threatened March on Washington Movement pressured FDR into signing it.
p2: Banned racial discrimination in the defence industries.
p3: Over 2 million African Americans were employed in defence work by the war's end.

front: How did WWII service expose America's own hypocrisy?
p1: Fighting for democracy abroad while denied it at home exposed a glaring contradiction, sparking new activism like CORE's founding (1942).
p2: Over 1 million African Americans served; the Tuskegee Airmen proved their skill in combat.
p3: Segregation persisted for three years after the war, until Truman's Executive Order 9981 (1948).

front: What did Smith v Allwright (1944) achieve?
p1: Outlawed all-white primary elections across the South.
p2: Black voter registration rose from 2% in 1940 to 12% by 1947.
p3: A genuine, if still modest, step forward for Southern Black voting rights.

front: What was the impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
p1: Built on Gaines v Canada (1938), which first ruled facilities had to be genuinely equal.
p2: Overturned Plessy v Ferguson, ruling school segregation unconstitutional.
p3: Marshall proved Southern states spent $43 a year on Black pupils, $179 on white.

front: How did the South resist Brown v Board?
p1: Brown II (1956) set no real deadline, only 'all deliberate speed'.
p2: Virginia closed all its public schools in 1956 rather than integrate them.
p3: Brown's ruling theoretically affected 9 million children, but changed almost nothing in practice.

front: What were the White Citizens' Councils?
p1: Formed in 1955 in direct response to Brown v Board.
p2: Known as the 'Uptown Klan' for pursuing the same goals through respectable means.
p3: Used economic pressure — sackings, evictions — reaching 60,000 members by the late 1950s.

front: What happened during the Little Rock Nine crisis (1957)?
p1: Governor Faubus deployed the Arkansas National Guard to block their integration.
p2: Eisenhower responded by deploying the 101st Airborne to enforce it.
p3: First direct federal force protecting Black civil rights since Reconstruction.

front: What was the impact of the Emmett Till case (1955)?
p1: 14-year-old boy brutally murdered in Mississippi.
p2: His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral, letting the media share his image.
p3: Galvanised the civil rights movement into wider, more urgent action.

front: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott change the direction of the movement?
p1: Sparked by Rosa Parks' arrest for refusing to give up her bus seat.
p2: 381-day boycott by 40,000 Black residents of Montgomery, led by King.
p3: Cost the bus company $3,000 a day, which was what actually forced it to desegregate.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the SCLC?
p1: Formed 1957, led by Martin Luther King, committed to non-violent methods.
p2: Built directly on the momentum and organisation of the Montgomery boycott.
p3: 1957 Civil Rights Act followed the same year, but was only weakly enforced.

front: What were the Greensboro Sit-ins (1960) and why were they significant?
p1: Four Black students sat at a 'whites-only' lunch counter in North Carolina.
p2: 70,000 students joined similar sit-ins across the South.
p3: Over 1,000 businesses desegregated their lunch counters as a result.

front: What was the strategy and significance of SNCC?
p1: Founded 1960, grassroots and student-led — more radical than the SCLC.
p2: Grew directly out of the momentum of the Greensboro sit-ins.
p3: 1966: Carmichael took over, rejecting non-violence and coining 'Black Power'.

front: What were the Freedom Rides (1961) and what did they achieve?
p1: CORE and SNCC activists rode interstate buses into the Deep South to test the law.
p2: Tested Boynton v Virginia (1960), which had ruled interstate bus segregation unconstitutional.
p3: Met with mob violence and fire-bombing, forcing the Attorney General to enforce desegregation.

front: What was the Albany Campaign (1962) and why did it fail?
p1: SCLC targeted Albany, Georgia; Police Chief Pritchett used deliberately restrained policing.
p2: No single dramatic confrontation meant the media lost interest.
p3: Key lesson: non-violence only worked when it provoked visible brutality on camera.

front: What happened at Ole Miss (1962)?
p1: James Meredith attempted to enrol at the University of Mississippi.
p2: Riots broke out as the state governor tried to block his enrolment.
p3: Kennedy sent 30,000 federal troops to enforce it.

front: How did the Birmingham Campaign force federal action?
p1: King and SCLC deliberately targeted Birmingham, expecting Bull Connor's brutality.
p2: Connor's police dogs and fire hoses against child protesters were broadcast worldwide.
p3: Kennedy announced America had a 'moral duty' to act — leading directly to the Civil Rights Act.

front: What was the impact of the 16th Street Baptist Church bombing (1963)?
p1: KKK bombed a Black church in Birmingham, killing four young girls.
p2: No convictions followed for over a decade.
p3: Shocked the nation into recognising the movement's non-violence against real, deadly danger.

front: Why is the March on Washington remembered as a turning point?
p1: 250,000 marched for jobs and freedom; King delivered 'I Have a Dream'.
p2: Organised by Randolph and Rustin, uniting the NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE and NUL.
p3: Malcolm X dismissed it as a 'farce', exposing splits within the movement.

front: What was George Wallace's role as an opponent of civil rights?
p1: As Governor of Alabama, pledged 'segregation now, tomorrow, forever'.
p2: Stood in the doorway of the University of Alabama in 1963 to block Black students.
p3: Encouraged Bull Connor's violent tactics during the Birmingham Campaign.

front: How did Southern states resist integration through the 1960s?
p1: State governments funded private 'segregation academies' to avoid integrating public schools.
p2: Over 300 had been founded by the late 1960s.
p3: Let white families avoid desegregated schools entirely, legally.

front: What was the impact of the Civil Rights Act (1964)?
p1: Removed legal segregation across the South and banned employment discrimination.
p2: Passed using LBJ's personal pressure — the 'Johnson treatment'.
p3: BUT did not address de facto segregation or economic inequality in the North.

front: What happened during the Selma March and what did it achieve?
p1: Selma: 50% Black population but only 1% could vote.
p2: John Lewis led marchers attacked by Sheriff Jim Clark's police ('Bloody Sunday'), broadcast nationally.
p3: Led directly to the Voting Rights Act, banning poll taxes and literacy tests outright.

front: What was the impact of the Voting Rights Act (1965)?
p1: Banned all remaining voter suppression methods outright.
p2: Mississippi's Black voter registration rose from 6% in 1964 to 60% by 1969.
p3: The single most effective piece of civil rights legislation of the whole period.

front: What did the Watts Riots reveal about the limits of civil rights legislation?
p1: Broke out in Los Angeles just days after the Voting Rights Act was signed.
p2: Response to poverty, police brutality and de facto segregation, not Southern-style Jim Crow.
p3: $40 million in property damage — showed legal equality hadn't reached Northern ghettos.

front: What was the impact of the Great Society and Civil Rights Act on African Americans?
p1: Medicare and Medicaid (1965) raised Black hospital access from 25% to 75%; Food Stamps reached 33% of recipients.
p2: Civil Rights Act's EEOC enforcement raised Black white-collar workers from 5% to 15%.
p3: BUT by 1970, Black families still earned only 58% of white family income.

front: What roles did Black leaders play during the Great Society?
p1: Adam Clayton Powell Jr. chaired the House Education and Labour Committee.
p2: Martin Luther King worked directly with Johnson on the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts.
p3: Whitney Young of the NUL advised Johnson on anti-poverty policy.

front: How did Black political representation grow after the Voting Rights Act?
p1: Thurgood Marshall became the first Black Supreme Court Justice in 1967.
p2: Shirley Chisholm became the first Black woman in Congress in 1968.
p3: By the 1970s, Detroit, Atlanta and Washington DC all had Black mayors.

front: What was Malcolm X's positive impact as a civil rights leader?
p1: Grew the Nation of Islam from 400 members in 1952 to 40,000 by 1960.
p2: Addressed urban poverty in the North, where King's Southern appeal struggled.
p3: Assassinated by NOI members in 1965, after his 1964 Hajj had already softened his views.

front: What were the limitations of Malcolm X's impact?
p1: Unlike King, achieved no legislative victories at all.
p2: His separatist stance and 'by any means necessary' philosophy alienated moderates.
p3: Dismissed the March on Washington as a 'farce', alienating other civil rights leaders.

front: How did the Vietnam War fuel the rise of Black Power?
p1: African Americans were disproportionately drafted, returning radicalised and angry.
p2: King's 1967 'Beyond Vietnam' speech severed his relationship with Johnson.
p3: Media attention shifted from civil rights marches to anti-war protests.

front: How did the civil rights movement's failures in the North fuel Black Power?
p1: SCLC and NAACP focused on Southern desegregation, neglecting Northern communities.
p2: Despite the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts, urban poverty and police violence continued.
p3: King's non-violence was increasingly seen as ineffective against Northern systemic neglect.

front: How did the Long Hot Summers fuel the rise of Black Power?
p1: The Watts Riot (1965) exposed non-violence's failure to fix urban conditions.
p2: Many rioters saw Malcolm X's rhetoric as more realistic than King's vision.
p3: Police brutality drew growing support for Black Power's emphasis on self-defence.

front: What was the impact of the Black Panther Party's community programmes?
p1: Free breakfast programmes fed 20,000 children weekly.
p2: Ran 13 health clinics, screening thousands for sickle cell anaemia.
p3: Ten-Point Programme demanded reparations, land, full employment and decent housing.

front: What was the cultural impact of Black Power?
p1: Afro hairstyles and dashikis became acts of pride, not just fashion.
p2: Radicalised King himself, pushing the SCLC toward economic and social issues by the late 1960s.
p3: Inspired other movements too, including Native American activism, Latino groups and feminism.

front: What were the negatives of Black Power's impact?
p1: Fragmentation — no unified goal between cultural pride, armed defence and economic reform.
p2: COINTELPRO infiltration led to arrests and assassinations, including Fred Hampton (1969).
p3: The Panthers never exceeded 5,000 members, far short of King's mass movement.

front: How did Black Power alienate the movement's allies?
p1: Confrontational tone alienated white liberals and moderate African Americans.
p2: In 1969, CORE's white funding collapsed as it turned toward Black nationalism.
p3: Media images of armed Panthers made the movement look violent and chaotic.

front: What was the political position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: Black voter turnout reached 54%, against 61% for white Americans.
p2: Unofficial suppression continued — gerrymandering and too few polling stations in Black areas.
p3: Douglas Wilder became the first Black state governor, in Virginia, in 1989.

front: How much did Black political representation grow by 1992?
p1: Over 8,000 African Americans held office at every level of government.
p2: The Congressional Black Caucus, founded 1971, had grown to 36 members.
p3: BUT no African American had ever been a major party's presidential nominee.

front: How far did Jesse Jackson's campaigns break new political ground?
p1: Ran for the Democratic nomination in both 1984 and 1988.
p2: Won 7 million votes combined across both campaigns.
p3: BUT never became the party's official candidate.

front: What was the state of school integration by 1992?
p1: Desegregation peaked in the 1970s but reversed as courts weakened bussing in the 1980s.
p2: By 1992, around 40% of Black students attended majority-Black schools again.
p3: HBCUs remained vital, producing 25% of all Black graduates.

front: What were living standards like for African Americans by 1992?
p1: Medicaid, Medicare and housing assistance had genuinely improved conditions.
p2: BUT 33% of African Americans lived below the poverty line, against 12% of white Americans.
p3: Public housing projects often concentrated poverty rather than solving it.

front: What violence and prejudice did African Americans still face by 1992?
p1: Rodney King's beating (1991) and the LA Riots (1992) exposed continuing police brutality.
p2: The KKK still existed and continued to threaten Black communities.
p3: BUT such hate crimes were now rarer and met with far harsher legal consequences.

front: What was the cultural position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: Oprah Winfrey, Michael Jordan and Spike Lee became icons of Black success.
p2: Represented a genuine shift in mainstream visibility and achievement.
p3: BUT racist stereotypes persisted in wider media portrayals.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: Earned 60% of average white income, overrepresented in low-wage sectors.
p2: Unemployment stood at 14.2%, against 7.2% for white Americans.
p3: Homeownership was 43%, against 70% for white Americans — the legacy of redlining.

front: How much of a Black middle class and business class existed by 1992?
p1: Around 40% of African Americans were considered middle class.
p2: African Americans owned over 500,000 businesses.
p3: Combined gross revenue of these businesses exceeded $10 billion.

front: What was the position of African Americans in labour unions by 1992?
p1: Exclusion from unions had decreased, though real discrimination remained.
p2: Made up 11% of union membership, roughly matching their share of the population.
p3: BUT remained underrepresented in union leadership roles.

front: Who founded the Black Panther Party (1966)?
p1: Founded by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale.
p2: Combined Black Power, self-defence and socialist community support in one platform.
p3: Marked a clear break from the SCLC and NAACP's earlier strategies.

front: What happened during the Chicago Freedom Movement (1966)?
p1: King attempted to challenge de facto housing segregation in the North.
p2: Faced fierce, sometimes violent resistance from white Chicago residents.
p3: Failed to make real progress, exposing the limits of his Southern strategy up North.

front: What was the impact of Martin Luther King's assassination (1968)?
p1: Assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee.
p2: Triggered a new wave of race riots across American cities.
p3: Removed the movement's most unifying non-violent leader at a critical moment.

front: How did Nixon respond to the civil rights movement politically?
p1: Won the 1968 presidential election on a 'Law and Order' platform.
p2: Coded rhetoric appealed to white voters uneasy about recent unrest.
p3: Signalled a harder political line just as Black Power was at its peak.

front: How was affirmative action introduced and confirmed by the courts?
p1: First introduced by the federal government as a test in Philadelphia (1969).
p2: Griggs v Duke Power Co. (1971) confirmed it was constitutional.
p3: Spread nationally, raising Black white-collar employment from 5% to 15% by the mid-1970s.

front: What did Swann v Charlotte-Mecklenburg (1971) establish?
p1: Ruled that court-ordered bussing to integrate schools was constitutional.
p2: Led to real change — 90% of Black children attended integrated schools by 1972.
p3: BUT support for bussing weakened through the 1970s regardless.

front: What did Regents of the University of California v Bakke (1978) decide?
p1: Ruled that strict racial quotas in university admissions were unconstitutional.
p2: Race could still be considered as one factor among several.
p3: Significantly weakened affirmative action's legal foundation going forward.

front: What was the impact of the War on Drugs on African Americans?
p1: Launched by Nixon in 1971, expanded significantly by Reagan in the 1980s.
p2: Imposed harsh mandatory minimum sentences, disproportionately targeting Black communities.
p3: By 1992, 25% of Black men were in prison, on parole or on probation.

front: What was the impact of Reagan's welfare cuts in the 1980s?
p1: Cut welfare programmes that disproportionately supported African Americans.
p2: Deepened existing economic disparities rather than closing them.
p3: Combined with War on Drugs sentencing to entrench Black poverty further.

front: How did the Michael Donald case end differently from lynchings before it?
p1: A rare lynching this late in the period, carried out by the Alabama KKK.
p2: Resulted in a strong federal response — the murderer was found guilty and executed.
p3: Financial penalties from the case effectively bankrupted the Alabama KKK.

front: What was the legal position of unions in 1865?
p1: No legal protections for unions, and no obligation for employers to recognise them.
p2: Courts consistently ruled in employers' favour throughout the 1860s.
p3: 20 state governments had laws allowing militias to intervene in labour disputes by the 1870s.

front: What was the NLU, and why did it collapse so quickly?
p1: Founded 1866 by William Sylvis, reaching 300,000 members at its peak.
p2: Collapsed after Sylvis's death in 1869.
p3: Even successful craft unions like the Cigar Makers covered under 10% of any industry's workers.

front: Why did strikes routinely fail in 1865?
p1: Fewer than 5% of strikes led to any concessions between 1865 and 1875.
p2: Scab labour was widespread — 20 to 30 replacements for every 100 strikers.
p3: Blacklisting was common — in Pennsylvania, shared among 50 mine operators.

front: What happened with the Molly Maguires (1873)?
p1: Violent conflict between Irish labourers and mine owners in Pennsylvania's coalfields.
p2: Pinkerton detectives infiltrated the group to gather evidence against them.
p3: 10 leaders were arrested and executed in 1876.

front: How were strikes treated by the press and courts in 1865?
p1: Newspapers branded strikers as 'rioters' or 'anarchists'.
p2: Courts issued injunctions against strikes across 200,000 miles of privately-owned railroad track.
p3: Together, this made sustained strike action almost impossible to maintain.

front: How dangerous and unregulated was industrial work in 1865?
p1: 50% of the American workforce worked in manufacturing or mining by 1870.
p2: 3,000 railroad workers were killed and 20,000 injured annually from unsafe conditions.
p3: 750,000 children under 15 worked in industrial labour, some from age 8 in 12-hour shifts.

front: How unequal was pay across different groups of workers in 1865?
p1: Most African Americans in the South worked as sharecroppers, earning as little as 50 cents a day.
p2: Women made up 15% of the industrial workforce, earning $3–6 a week against $7–10 for men.
p3: Immigrants worked 60–70 hour weeks in sweatshops for as little as $1 a day.

front: What safety net existed for injured or unemployed workers in 1865?
p1: Average industrial wages were just $1–2 a day.
p2: No legal framework existed for employer-provided healthcare or injury compensation.
p3: Immigrant workers were often barred from union membership entirely, compounding their exclusion.

front: What did the NLU actually campaign for, and why did it fail?
p1: Sylvis pushed for an 8-hour workday and broader legislative reforms.
p2: Undermined by the early 1870s depression and internal divisions between factions.
p3: Over-reliant on Sylvis personally — it never survived his death.

front: Why was the CNLU formed separately from the NLU?
p1: Formed in 1869 by African American workers excluded from the NLU.
p2: Reflected the NLU's own failure to organise across racial lines.
p3: Remained short-lived, without the NLU's national reach.

front: What made the Knights of Labor different when it was founded in 1869?
p1: Uniquely inclusive — welcomed women, African Americans and unskilled workers.
p2: Went on to become the largest labour organisation of the whole 19th century.
p3: A deliberate contrast to the NLU's narrower, more skilled-worker focus.

front: What happened during the Great Railroad Strike (1877)?
p1: Spontaneous strike after wage cuts during an economic depression, spreading from West Virginia.
p2: Workers shut down rail traffic across multiple companies at once.
p3: Federal troops killed over 100 workers, ending the strike in failure.

front: Why was the Great Railroad Strike historically significant, beyond its failure?
p1: The first genuinely nationwide labour dispute in American history.
p2: Exposed the urgent need for stronger, better-organised unions.
p3: Confirmed that federal violence was the government's default response to strikes.

front: How did the Haymarket Affair damage the union movement's public image?
p1: A bomb at a Chicago KOL rally for the 8-hour workday killed seven police and four civilians.
p2: Labour leaders were executed despite thin evidence linking them to the bombing.
p3: Discredited the Knights of Labor and linked unions with anarchism in the public mind.

front: How did the Homestead Strike expose the limits of union power?
p1: Wage cuts and anti-union actions at Carnegie's steelworks led the Amalgamated Association to clash with Pinkerton agents.
p2: 12 men died in the violence before 8,000 state militia crushed the strike.
p3: Kept the steel industry union-free for the next four decades.

front: How did the federal government respond to the Pullman Strike?
p1: Workers refused to handle Pullman cars after wage cuts with no reduction in their company-town rents.
p2: Debs and the ARU led the strike; a federal court injunction ruled it illegal.
p3: President Cleveland sent federal troops, crushing the strike by force.

front: Why did Eugene Debs become such an influential figure in union history?
p1: Led the first successful industrial union, uniting workers across a whole industry.
p2: His defeat in the Pullman Strike brought national attention to workers' struggles regardless.
p3: Later ran for president as a Socialist multiple times, winning 6% of the vote in 1912.

front: How did the AFL's approach differ from earlier unions?
p1: Led by Samuel Gompers, focused narrowly on skilled craft workers.
p2: Prioritised collective bargaining over radical demands, unlike the KOL.
p3: Achieved real negotiations with capitalists like Mark Hanna and J.P. Morgan.

front: How much did industrialisation benefit workers in the Gilded Age?
p1: Average industrial wages rose 48%, from $380 in 1880 to $564 by 1890.
p2: The industrial workforce grew from 885,000 in 1860 to 3 million by 1900.
p3: The Knights of Labor grew from 20,000 members in 1881 to 700,000 by 1886.

front: What were the limits of industrialisation's benefits for workers?
p1: 2,000 rail workers were killed in accidents in 1889 alone.
p2: 2% of the population owned 30% of the nation's wealth.
p3: Unskilled workers earned only 30% of what skilled workers earned.

front: How effective was the union movement that emerged in the Gilded Age?
p1: KOL and AFL gave workers real national frameworks for collective action for the first time.
p2: KOL and AFL both included women and African Americans, building broader solidarity.
p3: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) marked the start of federal intervention in business, however limited.

front: Why was the Gilded Age union movement still largely ineffective?
p1: Violent strikes like Pullman alienated the middle class and ended in failure.
p2: Homestead and others failed to secure lasting gains — steel stayed union-free into the 1930s.
p3: Courts increasingly issued injunctions to end strikes, especially after 1894.

front: How did government policy weaken labour's position in the Gilded Age?
p1: A laissez-faire attitude let corporations dominate without protective legislation.
p2: Court injunctions consistently favoured employers over striking workers.
p3: The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) was rarely used against monopolies — mostly against unions instead.

front: How did employer tactics weaken labour's position in the Gilded Age?
p1: Employers used blacklisting, strike-breakers and armed Pinkerton agents.
p2: Companies like Carnegie Steel deployed private militias against their own workers.
p3: Company towns like Pullman's let employers control workers' rents, wages and even newspapers.

front: How did divisions among workers themselves weaken the labour movement?
p1: 11 million new immigrants created wage competition, provoking nativist hostility.
p2: Skilled-worker unions often excluded the unskilled, women and immigrants.
p3: Many unions refused African American membership entirely, weakening overall solidarity.

front: What was the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882), and who supported it?
p1: Banned Chinese immigration, further marginalising Chinese workers in railroads and mining.
p2: Passed with major support from the KOL, despite its otherwise inclusive reputation.
p3: Showed even progressive unions could turn nativist when it suited their own members.

front: How did the Great Coal Strike change the government's role in strikes?
p1: John Mitchell led 140,000 UMWA miners demanding higher pay, shorter hours and safety.
p2: Roosevelt intervened directly, the first time government mediated rather than suppressed a strike.
p3: Resulted only in a compromise — a wage rise, but not full union recognition.

front: What happened during the Lawrence Textile Strike (1912)?
p1: Led by the IWW after a new law cut hours, prompting employers to cut wages to match.
p2: Sending strikers' children away for safety won huge public sympathy nationwide.
p3: Employers secretly planted dynamite, hoping to frame strikers as violent.

front: Why was the Lawrence Textile Strike (1912) significant?
p1: The dynamite plot was exposed, badly backfiring on the company's public image.
p2: Won a 15% pay rise and overtime pay, with no reprisals against strikers.
p3: Showed the power of women-led strikes and cross-ethnic solidarity among immigrant workers.

front: How did the Triangle Shirtwaist fire expose factory conditions?
p1: Killed 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women.
p2: Exposed how little factory owners had invested in basic safety standards.
p3: Directly pushed forward the case for workplace safety regulation.

front: How did the courts undermine labour rights in the Progressive Era?
p1: Lochner v New York (1905): struck down a law limiting bakers' hours, citing 'freedom of contract'.
p2: Coppage v Kansas (1915): upheld 'yellow-dog contracts' banning workers from joining unions.
p3: Both rulings showed courts consistently prioritised business freedom over worker protection.

front: How did Wilson's government try to improve labour relations?
p1: Established the Department of Labor (1913) to mediate disputes.
p2: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914) attempted to exempt unions from antitrust prosecution.
p3: BUT later court rulings undermined the Act's real-world protection anyway.

front: How did employers resist unions differently in the Progressive Era?
p1: Enforced 'open shop' policies, refusing to hire committed union members.
p2: Routinely fired workers suspected of organising.
p3: Introduced only token safety measures, mainly to limit legal liability.

front: How did WWI temporarily boost union recognition?
p1: Wilson's National War Labor Board (1918) set labour standards and settled disputes.
p2: Worked directly with the AFL to maintain wartime production without major strikes.
p3: BUT its benefits went almost entirely to AFL unions, not unskilled or industrial workers.

front: What was the Seattle General Strike (1919) and why did it fail?
p1: Various unions (AFL and IWW) struck over wage stagnation after the war.
p2: Nearly every worker in Seattle joined for five days, maintaining essential services themselves.
p3: Ended without real gains, fuelling national fears of a Bolshevik-style revolution.

front: What was the Red Scare (1919), and how did it damage unions?
p1: The Bolshevik Revolution in Russia sparked fears of communist revolution spreading to America.
p2: Any union activity became viewed with deep public suspicion as a result.
p3: Media coverage of the Seattle Strike reinforced this hostile, anti-union mood.

front: What was Welfare Capitalism, and why did employers adopt it?
p1: Employers introduced pensions, healthcare and other benefits directly themselves.
p2: Deliberately designed to make traditional union membership feel unnecessary.
p3: Company unions spread widely, replacing independent unions with employer-controlled ones.

front: What other tactics weakened unions through the 1920s?
p1: Yellow-dog contracts, banning workers from joining a union, became commonplace.
p2: Courts continued to treat strikes and boycotts as illegal restraints of trade.
p3: Union membership fell from its 1920 peak of around 5 million.

front: What was the impact of the Wall Street Crash (1929) on workers?
p1: Triggered the Great Depression, devastating the wider American economy.
p2: Mass unemployment left workers with even less bargaining power than before.
p3: Set the stage for the New Deal's federal intervention just a few years later.

front: How strong was labour's position by 1932?
p1: AFL had grown to 3 million members despite the Depression's onset.
p2: Worker protests forced some partial recognition in coal, textile and garment industries.
p3: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932) banned yellow-dog contracts, a first real legal gain.

front: What limited labour's position by 1932?
p1: A decade of welfare capitalism and yellow-dog contracts had left unions weak.
p2: Only around 3 million workers were organised — a small fraction of the workforce.
p3: Unemployment reached 25% overall, and 50% for African Americans.

front: What did the Wagner Act (1935) actually achieve?
p1: Legally recognised workers' rights to unionise and collectively bargain for the first time.
p2: Created the NLRB to oversee disputes and reinstate unfairly dismissed workers.
p3: Union membership surged from 3.7 million in 1933 to 9 million by 1938.

front: What did the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) establish?
p1: Set a minimum wage of $25 a week for industrial workers.
p2: Banned child labour under the age of 16 nationwide.
p3: BUT failed to address gender pay disparities, leaving women underpaid regardless.

front: What made the CIO different when it was founded in 1935?
p1: Took a broader, more inclusive approach, targeting unskilled workers directly.
p2: Actively organised women and African Americans, unlike the AFL.
p3: Grew to 3.7 million members by 1944, diversifying the whole labour movement.

front: What did the Flint Sit-Down Strikes (1936–37) achieve?
p1: Workers occupied General Motors plants, halting production entirely.
p2: Forced recognition of the United Auto Workers after a tense standoff.
p3: US Steel followed in 1937, unionising without a strike — 45 years after Homestead's failure.

front: What were the limits of the New Deal's gains for workers?
p1: Wagner Act's closed shops inadvertently sidelined Black workers via AFL exclusion.
p2: Social Security Act (1935) excluded domestic and farm workers, many of them Black.
p3: CIO welcomed Black and women members, but rarely gave them real positions of power.

front: How did Henry Ford resist the New Deal's labour reforms?
p1: Refused to recognise any union at his company for years after the Wagner Act.
p2: Held out until 1941, one of the very last major employers to accept organised labour.
p3: Showed individual employer resistance could outlast federal legislation for years.

front: How did the NRA and the courts resist New Deal labour reforms?
p1: Employers often ignored NRA codes while displaying its 'blue eagle' symbol regardless.
p2: Supreme Court struck down the NRA entirely in 1935.
p3: BUT the Wagner Act itself was upheld as constitutional in 1937 regardless.

front: How did violence against strikers play out differently in two 1930s cases?
p1: Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 steelworkers, causing national outrage.
p2: Textile Workers' Strike (1934): 400,000 workers were crushed anyway, with no such backlash.
p3: Showed violence could backfire badly in one case, yet still succeed completely in another.

front: Why did Southern opposition to the New Deal remain so strong?
p1: Black workers attempting to organise faced violent repression across the South.
p2: Sharecropper strikes achieved little without any real federal enforcement there.
p3: The New Deal never seriously challenged workplace segregation itself.

front: How did the WWII-era National War Labor Board affect unions?
p1: Government, employers, AFL and CIO worked together to mediate labour disputes.
p2: Unions agreed no-strike pledges in exchange for wartime recognition.
p3: Union membership reached its historic peak — 35% of the workforce by 1945.

front: What was the Smith-Connally Act (1943)?
p1: Let the federal government seize and run industries threatened by strike action.
p2: Passed specifically to prevent wartime production being disrupted.
p3: Passed over Roosevelt's own veto, showing Congress's growing anti-strike mood.

front: What was the post-war strike wave of 1946?
p1: 5,000 strikes broke out, involving 4.6 million workers nationwide.
p2: Workers pushed to recover wages lost to wartime wage controls.
p3: Provoked a hostile political backlash against union power.

front: How did McCarthyism damage the labour movement?
p1: The second Red Scare (1946–50s) linked union activism directly to communism.
p2: Fostered deep suspicion and division within the movement itself.
p3: Weakened unions' broader political influence at exactly the wrong moment.

front: What did the Taft-Hartley Act (1947) actually change?
p1: Banned secondary strikes and closed shops, both previously protected by the Wagner Act.
p2: Required union leaders to swear they were not communists.
p3: Passed over Truman's veto, significantly weakening the CIO in particular.

front: How far did the AFL-CIO merger unite the labour movement?
p1: Ended 20 years of rivalry between the two federations.
p2: Combined membership reached 15 million workers.
p3: BUT Black and women workers remained largely excluded from real leadership.

front: What did the Landrum-Griffin Act (1959) regulate?
p1: Required unions to publicly disclose their finances.
p2: Introduced new rules to protect union members from corrupt leadership.
p3: Further restricted secondary boycotts, building on Taft-Hartley's limits.

front: What did Kennedy's Executive Order 10988 (1962) achieve?
p1: Gave federal employees the right to organise and bargain collectively.
p2: A significant expansion, since federal workers had previously been excluded.
p3: Triggered rapid growth in public-sector union membership through the 1960s.

front: How did Chavez organise farm workers excluded from the law?
p1: Chavez founded the UFW to organise migrant farm workers, excluded from the NLRA.
p2: Led a five-year strike and consumer boycott against Californian grape growers.
p3: Won contracts covering wages and conditions, a rare victory for farm labour.

front: What was the Salad Bowl Strike (1970)?
p1: The largest farm worker strike in American history.
p2: UFW clashed directly with the Teamsters over rival contracts with growers.
p3: Showed farm labour organising could win real gains despite legal exclusion.

front: What did 1960s civil rights legislation do for workplace equality?
p1: Equal Pay Act (1963) banned paying women less for the same work.
p2: Civil Rights Act's Title VII (1964) banned employment discrimination by race and sex.
p3: BUT enforcement remained weak, and real pay gaps persisted regardless.

front: What did OSHA (1970) establish?
p1: Set binding federal workplace safety standards for the first time.
p2: Gave the government real power to inspect workplaces and issue fines.
p3: A direct legislative legacy of decades of unsafe conditions like Triangle Shirtwaist.

front: What gains did DRUM and the LRBW achieve for Black workers?
p1: DRUM (1968) organised successful wildcat strikes at Chrysler's Dodge Main plant.
p2: Inspired similar groups like FRUM and CADRUM across other auto plants.
p3: LRBW pushed for Black leadership, reaching 30% of UAW membership by the early 1970s.

front: How did Black Power reshape the priorities of the wider labour movement?
p1: Highlighted that over 50% of Black autoworkers in Detroit held the most dangerous jobs.
p2: Black Workers Congress (1971) coordinated demands for fair union representation.
p3: Shifted unions from focusing purely on race toward economic rights alongside it.

front: What limited the impact of DRUM and the LRBW?
p1: Focus on Black solidarity clashed with efforts to unite Black and white workers.
p2: Violent clashes with police alienated moderate Black leaders and white workers alike.
p3: Internal divisions caused both groups to collapse by the early 1970s.

front: How wide was the gap between Black workers and the wider UAW membership?
p1: Black autoworkers earned $2,000 a year less than white counterparts in the late 1960s.
p2: 70% of UAW members supported civil rights broadly.
p3: BUT only 5% supported the more radical demand for real Black leadership.

front: How did automation and deindustrialisation weaken unions in the 1970s–80s?
p1: Manufacturing jobs, historically the most heavily unionised, declined sharply.
p2: Factories closed or moved abroad, chasing cheaper non-union labour.
p3: Union membership fell steadily as the industrial workforce itself shrank.

front: How did the PATCO Strike change the government's approach to strikes?
p1: 11,000 air traffic controllers struck for better pay and working conditions.
p2: Reagan fired every striking controller and banned them from federal employment for life.
p3: Destroyed PATCO entirely and signalled a new era of hostility to strikes.

front: What was the impact of Reaganomics on the labour movement by 1992?
p1: Deregulation and tax cuts favoured business interests over organised labour.
p2: Reagan's own example emboldened private employers to resist unions more openly.
p3: Union membership fell to around 16% of the workforce by 1992.

front: What was the position of Native American land rights in 1865?
p1: South-eastern tribes had already been relocated to Indian Territory under the 1830s Removal Act.
p2: Plains tribes like the Sioux still held their land, but westward settlement sparked the Plains Wars.
p3: The Homestead Act (1862) granted settlers 160-acre plots, directly encroaching on Native land.

front: How did treaties and the railroad affect Native land in 1865?
p1: Treaties like Fort Laramie (1868) recognised land rights, but also confined tribes to shrinking areas.
p2: The transcontinental railroad (1869) opened the West to settlers, miners and ranchers.
p3: Government granted railway companies land taken directly from tribes.

front: What self-determination did Native American tribes still hold in 1865?
p1: Tribes were still largely self-governed, with chiefs holding real authority.
p2: The US government initially treated tribes as foreign nations, negotiating treaties with them.
p3: BUT these treaties were routinely violated once made.

front: How did the Bureau of Indian Affairs undermine self-determination?
p1: Managed Native affairs on behalf of the federal government.
p2: Acted paternalistically and often corruptly toward the tribes it oversaw.
p3: The growing settler influx left tribes with fewer means to resist federal control.

front: How did the US government attack Native cultural and religious freedom in 1865?
p1: Assimilation was promoted as the solution to the government's so-called 'Indian problem'.
p2: White Christian missionaries were sent to reservations to replace traditional spiritual practices.
p3: Ceremonies like the Sun Dance still continued, despite settler hostility toward them.

front: How did the buffalo's destruction affect Native American life?
p1: The railroad destroyed the buffalo's traditional migration patterns.
p2: The government deliberately encouraged buffalo hunting to force tribes onto reservations.
p3: Between 1860 and 1889, the buffalo population fell from 30 million to fewer than 1,000.

front: What was the political and economic position of Native Americans in 1865?
p1: Many lived in poverty on reservations, dependent on poor-quality government rations.
p2: Not recognised as US citizens, they had no political representation at all.
p3: Considered 'wards of the state', excluded from the economic opportunities of westward expansion.

front: What health crisis did Native Americans face in 1865?
p1: Faced disproportionately high rates of malnutrition and tuberculosis.
p2: Tuberculosis rates ran 25% higher than the national average.
p3: Alcoholism reached as high as 70% among men in some tribes.

front: What was the impact of the Civil War on Native Americans?
p1: Distracted federal attention, leaving settlers and militias free rein against Native resistance.
p2: Cherokee, Choctaw and Creek allied with the Confederacy for political and economic reasons.
p3: Alliances deepened divisions within Native communities and led to further relocation as punishment.

front: What happened during the Sand Creek Massacre and the Long Walk?
p1: Sand Creek (1864): Colorado militia killed 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women and children, despite their surrender.
p2: The Navajo's Long Walk (1864–66) forced relocation to Bosque Redondo.
p3: Caused widespread starvation and death among the Navajo during the journey.

front: What was the significance of Red Cloud's War (1866–68)?
p1: The Sioux defeated the US Army, a rare outright military victory.
p2: Forced the 2nd Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868), recognising Sioux control of the Black Hills.
p3: BUT the victory proved short-lived once gold was discovered there.

front: What was the significance of the Battle of Little Bighorn (1876)?
p1: Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse led Lakota Sioux and Cheyenne forces to defeat General Custer.
p2: A symbolic victory, widely seen as proof Native resistance could still succeed.
p3: BUT provoked a harsh US response that ended in the loss of the Black Hills.

front: What did the Indian Appropriations Act (1871) change?
p1: Declared tribes would no longer be recognised as independent nations.
p2: Ended the practice of negotiating treaties with tribes altogether.
p3: Reclassified Native Americans as 'wards of the state' instead.

front: How did the Dawes Act (1887) devastate Native land ownership?
p1: Divided communal tribal land into individual 160-acre allotments.
p2: Unallocated 'surplus' land was sold directly to white settlers.
p3: Native-owned land fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934.

front: How was the Dawes Act extended and worsened after 1887?
p1: Curtis Act (1898) extended allotment to the Five Civilised Tribes.
p2: Dead Indian Act (1902) let individuals sell inherited land, accelerating losses.
p3: Together, these dismantled tribal landholding far beyond the original Act's scope.

front: What was the Ghost Dance Movement, and how did it end?
p1: A religious revival (1889–90) promising the return of lost lands and the old way of life.
p2: Spread rapidly among Plains tribes desperate for hope after decades of loss.
p3: Suppressed violently at Wounded Knee (1890), where over 250 were killed.

front: What happened to Native children at boarding schools like Carlisle?
p1: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (1879) aimed to assimilate Native children by force.
p2: Over 100,000 children were forced into such schools by the early 1900s.
p3: Forbidden their languages and traditions, with death rates from neglect reaching 30–50%.

front: What was the long-term cultural cost of assimilation policy?
p1: Boarding schools deliberately imposed Western gender norms on tribes.
p2: This undermined matriarchal tribes like the Iroquois, where women traditionally managed land.
p3: By 1930, 75% of Native American languages had already been lost.

front: How did the courts erode tribal sovereignty by 1903?
p1: Crow Dog Case (1883) recognised tribal authority over crimes on reservations.
p2: Cherokee Nation v Hitchcock (1902) and the Major Crimes Act (1885) both confirmed federal control instead.
p3: Lone Wolf v Hitchcock (1903) then ruled Congress could break treaties unilaterally.

front: What was the Indian Rights Association, and what did it actually support?
p1: Founded in 1882, a year after Helen Hunt Jackson's 'A Century of Dishonor' exposed the mistreatment.
p2: Supported the Dawes Act's allotment policy as being 'for their own good'.
p3: In practice, helped fragment tribal landholding rather than protect it.

front: What was the Society of American Indians (1911)?
p1: The first Native-led national rights organisation.
p2: Advocated for citizenship, education and greater unity among tribes.
p3: BUT its own focus on assimilation limited how much genuine support it won.

front: What was the Sequoyah movement (1905)?
p1: The Five Civilised Tribes proposed an all-Native state within Indian Territory.
p2: Congress rejected the proposal outright.
p3: Oklahoma was created instead, absorbing the territory entirely.

front: What positive case can be made for reservations, using the Navajo as an example?
p1: Navajo reservation land expanded from 4 million to 10.5 million acres by 1900.
p2: Their sheep and goat numbers grew from 15,000 to 1.7 million in the same period.
p3: BIA-run schools at Santa Fe, Carson and Phoenix offered some genuine education.

front: What made most reservations "ghettos in the wilderness" instead?
p1: The BIA managing them was often corrupt or simply inefficient.
p2: Government meat subsidies were cut even as disease killed reservation cattle.
p3: By 1900, only 100,000 of an estimated 240,000 Plains Indians remained alive.

front: What was the significance of Native American service in WWI?
p1: Around 12,000 Native Americans served, 400 of them awarded the Medal of Honor.
p2: Served despite being denied full citizenship rights at home.
p3: Exposed the glaring contradiction of fighting for a democracy that excluded them.

front: What did AIDA achieve under John Collier?
p1: Founded in 1923 to protect Native lands and religious freedom.
p2: Successfully blocked the Leavitt Bill (1926), which sought to ban traditional dances.
p3: Mobilised public opinion around Native religious rights for the first time.

front: What did the Indian Citizenship Act (1924) actually achieve?
p1: Granted US citizenship to all Native Americans born in the country.
p2: BUT many states still barred them from voting under separate state laws.
p3: Citizenship alone did nothing to address poverty or land loss.

front: What did the Meriam Report (1928) expose?
p1: Documented the Dawes Act's failures in devastating detail.
p2: Highlighted the deep poverty and poor conditions on reservations.
p3: Directly called for reform in education, healthcare and land management.

front: How strong was the Native American position by 1932?
p1: All Native Americans now held US citizenship.
p2: BUT two-thirds of tribal land had been lost since the Dawes Act.
p3: Boarding schools housed 60,000 children, with under 5% reaching higher education.

front: What did the Indian Reorganization Act (1934) change?
p1: Allowed tribes to establish their own democratic constitutions and councils.
p2: Protected remaining land from sale and recovered some unallocated land.
p3: Overturned bans on ceremonial dances and protected religious use of peyote.

front: What economic programmes did the Indian Reorganization Act bring?
p1: CCC-Indian Division employed 85,000 Native Americans between 1933 and 1942.
p2: Planted over 25 million trees and built 6,500 miles of road on tribal lands.
p3: Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935) revived traditional arts as an economic venture.

front: Why was the Indian Reorganization Act's adoption so uneven?
p1: Only 174 of 252 tribes that voted actually accepted it; just 92 fully adopted it.
p2: Its secret ballot system clashed with traditional open council discussion.
p3: The Navajo rejected it outright after being forced to kill 150,000 sheep under separate livestock policy.

front: How limited was the Indian Reorganization Act's real impact?
p1: Land buyback funding totalled only $2 million a year, far too little to matter.
p2: Just 4 million of the 90 million acres lost were ever restored.
p3: Collier's own one-size-fits-all approach failed to account for real tribal diversity.

front: Did the New Deal represent real change for Native Americans, or mere continuity?
p1: Marked a genuine break from decades of assimilationist Dawes Act policy.
p2: BUT paternalistic federal decision-making persisted regardless.
p3: 82% of Native Americans still lived below the poverty line by 1940.

front: What was the significance of the Navajo Code Talkers in WWII?
p1: 400–500 Navajo Marines created an unbreakable code, among over 44,000 Native Americans serving overall.
p2: Ira Hayes, a Pima soldier, became a national icon after being photographed raising the flag at Iwo Jima.
p3: BUT neither brought lasting change — Hayes faced alcoholism and discrimination once he returned home.

front: How did WWII internment policy affect Native American land?
p1: Over 120,000 Japanese Americans were forcibly relocated to internment camps.
p2: Some of these camps were built directly on Native reservations.
p3: Built entirely without consulting the tribes whose land it was.

front: What did the NCAI and the Indian Claims Commission achieve?
p1: NCAI (1944) founded specifically to oppose future termination policies.
p2: Lobbied successfully for the Indian Claims Commission (1946) to hear land claims.
p3: Awarded over $800 million in compensation, but returned almost no land itself.

front: What did Harrison v Laveen (1948) achieve?
p1: Recognised Native Americans' constitutional right to vote.
p2: Directly challenged state-level laws still blocking that right.
p3: A genuine legal victory, decades after citizenship had technically been granted.

front: What was Termination Policy (1953), and what did it do?
p1: Over 100 tribes lost federal recognition entirely.
p2: Their lands were sold off as a direct result.
p3: Left affected communities in extreme poverty almost immediately.

front: What was the Indian Relocation Act (1956), and did it work?
p1: Encouraged Native Americans to move to cities in search of jobs.
p2: Some genuinely thrived in their new urban environment.
p3: BUT many ended up in poverty, disconnected from their cultural communities.

front: How deep was reservation poverty by the 1960s and 70s?
p1: Per capita income was often less than half the national average.
p2: Unemployment regularly surpassed 50% on many reservations.
p3: In some areas, unemployment reached as high as 80%.

front: What was the NIYC, and did it predate Black Power's influence?
p1: Founded in 1961, years before Black Power's peak militancy.
p2: Organised 'fish-ins' protesting violations of treaty-protected fishing rights.
p3: Showed Native activism was already developing independently of Black Power.

front: How did Black Power directly shape AIM's founding (1968)?
p1: Adopted red berets and black jackets, styled directly on the Black Panthers.
p2: The term 'Red Power' itself was a deliberate echo of 'Black Power'.
p3: Encouraged Pan-Indian unity, mirroring Black Power's push past tribal or racial divisions.

front: What happened during the Siege of Alcatraz (1969–71)?
p1: Led by Richard Oakes, occupying the island in the name of Native sovereignty.
p2: Around 10,000 Native Americans visited over the course of the occupation.
p3: Ended in 1971 without securing any real policy change.

front: What happened during the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972)?
p1: A cross-country caravan of activists converged on Washington DC.
p2: Occupied the Bureau of Indian Affairs headquarters itself.
p3: Issued a 20-point manifesto demanding sovereignty and treaty enforcement.

front: What happened during the Wounded Knee Occupation (1973)?
p1: 71-day standoff between AIM members and federal forces in South Dakota.
p2: Exposed real corruption within the Pine Ridge Reservation's own government.
p3: Gained international attention but ended violently, with several deaths.

front: What evidence suggests Red Power grew independently of Black Power?
p1: Resistance to termination and the Indian Claims Commission predated Black Power's rise.
p2: WWII-era groups like the NCAI were already organising before Black Power existed.
p3: Johnson and Kennedy's 'Great Society' and 'War on Poverty' laid separate groundwork.

front: What limited Red Power's real impact?
p1: Tensions between militant AIM and legally-focused NCAI weakened the movement's unity.
p2: Richard Oakes' death in 1972 left a real leadership vacuum.
p3: Its urban focus left rural, reservation-based Native Americans underrepresented.

front: What legislation did Red Power activism eventually help win?
p1: Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (1975): gave tribes federal-programme control.
p2: American Indian Religious Freedom Act (1978): protected sacred sites and traditional practices.
p3: Indian Child Welfare Act (1978): stopped Native children being removed into non-Native homes.

front: What did US v Sioux Nation (1980) decide?
p1: Ruled the US had illegally seized the Black Hills back in 1877.
p2: Awarded the Sioux $106 million in compensation.
p3: The Sioux refused the money outright, demanding the land itself back instead.

front: What was the position of Native American land rights by 1992?
p1: The Indian Claims Commission compensated some losses, but returned almost no land.
p2: Some land was returned through separate settlements, but these were rare.
p3: By 1992, around 30% of Native Americans still lived on land-restricted reservations.

front: How much genuine self-determination existed by 1992?
p1: Over 200 tribes had assumed control of their own federal programmes.
p2: BUT the federal government still controlled most of the actual funding.
p3: 60% of Native Americans remained economically reliant on federal assistance.

front: What was the state of Native cultural and religious freedom by 1992?
p1: Over 100 Native language programmes were actively preserving endangered languages.
p2: Native arts and crafts had become a genuine multi-million-dollar industry.
p3: BUT over 70% of religious leaders still struggled to freely access sacred sites.

front: How effective was the Native American Graves Protection Act (1990) by 1992?
p1: Required museums and federal agencies to return Native remains and artefacts.
p2: Around 10,000 items had already been returned by 1992.
p3: BUT far more remained held in private collections, entirely unaffected by the Act.

front: How did Native American gaming transform reservation economies by 1992?
p1: Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988) allowed tribes to run their own casinos.
p2: Around 150 casinos were operating by the early 1990s.
p3: Generated over $1 billion in annual revenue for the tribes involved.

front: What was the economic and social position of Native Americans by 1992?
p1: 25% of Native American families still lived below the poverty line.
p2: Under 60% graduated high school, and only around 10% held a college degree.
p3: Life expectancy remained 5 to 10 years shorter than the national average.

front: What was the political position of Native Americans by 1992?
p1: Held US citizenship, but voter disenfranchisement remained a real problem.
p2: Only around 50% of Native Americans were registered to vote.
p3: Turnout among those registered remained low regardless.

front: How did the 15th Amendment divide the women's movement in 1865?
p1: Granted African American men the vote but excluded women entirely.
p2: NWSA (Anthony and Stanton) opposed it, demanding a federal amendment for women instead.
p3: AWSA (Stone) took the opposite approach, campaigning state-by-state instead.

front: What early acts of political defiance did women take in 1865?
p1: Wyoming Territory (1869) granted women the vote, a rare exception nationally.
p2: Anthony attempted to vote in 1872, claiming a right under the 14th Amendment.
p3: Arrested and fined $100, she refused to pay it.

front: How did the 'cult of domesticity' shape women's lives in 1865?
p1: Confined women's role to home and family life.
p2: Marriage was society's cornerstone; once married, a woman's legal rights were subsumed by her husband.
p3: Some women formed 'Boston Marriages' instead — supportive partnerships outside this norm.

front: What was the reality of childbirth and reproduction for women in 1865?
p1: Comstock Laws (1873) made distributing contraceptive information illegal.
p2: Women had between 5 and 7 children on average during their lifetime.
p3: 1 in 5 women died during childbirth itself.

front: How much had women's employment grown by 1870?
p1: Employment outside the home rose from 6% of women in 1860 to 15% by 1870.
p2: Only 3% attended college by 1870, against 25% of men.
p3: BUT earned only half of what men made for the same work.

front: How did race and class shape women's economic experiences in 1865?
p1: 40% of African American women in the South worked in domestic service by 1870.
p2: Most unions excluded women entirely, though the KOL (1869) welcomed them.
p3: War widowhood, over 400,000 in the North alone, pushed many into this same low-paid work.

front: How much did women's education improve during the Gilded Age?
p1: Women in higher education rose from 21% of all students in 1870 to 32% by 1880.
p2: By 1900, half of all high school graduates were women.
p3: BUT education was often still framed as preparation for marriage, not real opportunity.

front: How much did women's employment change during the Gilded Age?
p1: By 1900, around 1 million women worked as teachers, secretaries and telephone operators.
p2: Clerical employment for women grew tenfold over this period.
p3: BUT immigrant factory women often worked 70-hour weeks for as little as $5.

front: How did domestic life change for women during the Gilded Age?
p1: Indoor plumbing, central heating and commercial laundries reduced household burdens.
p2: Let women balance work and home life more effectively than before.
p3: The average birth rate fell from 5.42 children in 1850 to 3.56 by 1900.

front: Why did most women still lack real rights by the end of the Gilded Age?
p1: Most women still had no access to suffrage anywhere in the country.
p2: Suffrage groups themselves struggled to build genuinely broad public support.
p3: Black women were largely excluded from the mainstream movement entirely.

front: How effective were the NWSA's tactics compared to Mother Jones' activism?
p1: NWSA used attention-grabbing tactics — attempting to vote, getting arrested.
p2: Mother Jones organised mine workers' strikes directly.
p3: Led a march of factory children in 1903 to protest child labour.

front: What was the significance of Hull House (1889)?
p1: Founded by Jane Addams to serve poor immigrant families in Chicago.
p2: Was already serving over 2,000 people a week within its second year.
p3: Became a national model for urban social reform more broadly.

front: What did the WCTU, NCL and YWCA each contribute?
p1: WCTU (1874, led by Willard from 1879) fought alcohol's social effects and promoted women's moral authority.
p2: National Consumers League (1899) pushed for better workplace conditions for women.
p3: YWCA (1867) helped young single women moving to cities find jobs and safe housing.

front: Why did women's labour organising remain so ineffective?
p1: Male-dominated unions often refused to support women's strikes at all.
p2: An 1882 Massachusetts textile strike over a pay cut received no male union support.
p3: By 1900, only 2% of trade unionists were women.

front: How did Ida B. Wells challenge the mainstream women's movement?
p1: Key figure in the National Association of Colored Women, founded 1896.
p2: Fought specifically for Black women's rights, often ignored by white-led groups.
p3: Showed the mainstream suffrage movement's limits were a choice, not an accident.

front: What united women across class lines during the Gilded Age?
p1: Growth in education and workforce participation touched both middle and working-class women.
p2: NWSA and AWSA, despite tactical differences, shared the same ultimate suffrage goal.
p3: Their combined efforts laid real groundwork for the eventual 19th Amendment.

front: What divided women during the Gilded Age?
p1: Working-class and immigrant women had little solidarity with middle-class reformers.
p2: Many immigrant women worked 70-hour sweatshop weeks while others campaigned for reform instead.
p3: Widespread hostility framed working women as a threat to male breadwinners.

front: What was distinctive about Alice Paul's approach to suffrage?
p1: Founded the Congressional Union with Lucy Burns in 1913.
p2: Adopted militant, direct-action tactics modelled on British suffragettes.
p3: Demanded a federal constitutional amendment rather than a state-by-state campaign.

front: How did the Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911) affect women specifically?
p1: Killed 146 garment workers, the overwhelming majority of them women.
p2: Exposed how little protection existed for women in factory work.
p3: Spurred a wave of safety regulation aimed specifically at protecting women workers.

front: What was the significance of the Bread and Roses Strike (1912)?
p1: Led by immigrant women in Lawrence, Massachusetts, demanding fair wages.
p2: Around 20,000 workers took part in the strike.
p3: Won real wage increases and improved conditions for many women.
