front: How did Margaret Sanger campaign for birth control?
p1: Opened her first clinic in Brooklyn (1916), serving over 20,000 women.
p2: Shut down for violating the Comstock Laws' ban on contraceptive information.
p3: Founded the American Birth Control League (1921), later Planned Parenthood.

front: What was the significance of Jeannette Rankin?
p1: Became the first woman elected to Congress in 1916, representing Montana.
p2: An ardent supporter of women's rights throughout her career.
p3: Achieved this three years before women nationally even won the vote.

front: How did WWI change women's role in the workforce?
p1: Women's employment rate rose to approximately 40% during the war.
p2: Entered traditionally male-dominated industrial and clerical roles.
p3: Proved their capability in work previously assumed to be beyond them.

front: What role did NAWSA play in winning the vote?
p1: Formed in 1890 by merging the NWSA and AWSA under Carrie Chapman Catt.
p2: Grew to 2 million members by 1919.
p3: Played the pivotal role in finally securing the 19th Amendment's passage.

front: What did the 19th Amendment (1920) actually achieve?
p1: Granted women the vote after decades of sustained campaigning.
p2: BUT only around a third of women actually voted, against two-thirds of men.
p3: Black women in the South still faced the same voter suppression men did.

front: How limited were the gains of the early 1920s for women?
p1: Women's Bureau (1920) was created but given very limited enforcement powers.
p2: Shepard-Towner Act (1921) funded maternal health, but funding was cut by 1929.
p3: Flapper culture challenged gender norms, but mainly for white, middle-class women.

front: What political gains had women made by 1932?
p1: Nellie Taylor Ross became the first female state governor, in Wyoming (1925–27).
p2: Alice Paul's National Woman's Party proposed the ERA in 1923.
p3: Though it failed, it stimulated real debate around women's legal equality.

front: What workforce and reproductive gains had women made by 1932?
p1: Women's Bureau (1920) actively advocated for better working conditions.
p2: More women entered clerical and white-collar jobs through the 1920s.
p3: Sanger's birth control clinics spread public awareness of contraception.

front: What economic limitations did women still face by 1932?
p1: Confined mostly to low-paid 'feminised' jobs like teaching and nursing.
p2: Women in manufacturing earned around half of what men earned for the same work.
p3: Married women were often the first fired once the Depression hit.

front: What social limitations did women still face by 1932?
p1: Contraception remained illegal in many states under the Comstock Laws.
p2: Access to birth control was largely limited to wealthier, urban women.
p3: Public opinion still idealised women purely as homemakers and caregivers.

front: Which women reached senior government positions under the New Deal?
p1: Frances Perkins became the first female Cabinet member, Secretary of Labor 1933–45.
p2: Florence Allen became the first female US Circuit Court judge.
p3: Nellie Taylor Ross went on to direct the US Mint.

front: How much did the New Deal expand women's employment?
p1: Women's union membership reached 800,000 by 1940, a 300% rise since 1930.
p2: WPA employed over 400,000 women by 1938.
p3: Brought real financial stability to many families otherwise without income.

front: How did the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) still fail women?
p1: Set a minimum wage, but reinforced rather than closed the gender pay gap.
p2: Female teachers earned 20% less than male teachers as late as 1939.
p3: Domestic and agricultural workers, disproportionately women of colour, were excluded entirely.

front: How did New Deal relief programmes still assume men were the breadwinners?
p1: CCC excluded women from its programmes altogether.
p2: WPA limited public employment to just one family member, favouring men.
p3: 80% of Americans in a 1936 Gallup poll opposed married women working at all.

front: In what ways was the New Deal experience universal for women?
p1: All faced societal pressure reinforcing homemaking as their primary role.
p2: The 1936 Gallup poll's hostility to married women working cut across race and class.
p3: Most women, whatever their background, remained shut out of higher-paying jobs and real political power.

front: How differently did women experience the New Deal depending on race?
p1: Black women were excluded from relief programmes, but Bethune gave them a real voice.
p2: Mexican American women faced discrimination and deportation risk in public works schemes.
p3: Native American women gained limited job training from the Indian Reorganization Act, but stayed outside mainstream New Deal networks.

front: How much did WWII change women's employment?
p1: 6 million women entered the civilian workforce; 350,000 more served in non-combat military roles.
p2: By 1944, a quarter of women worked outside the home, up from just one in ten in 1940.
p3: 'Rosie the Riveter' became the iconic image of women's industrial contribution.

front: What happened to women who wanted to keep working after WWII ended?
p1: 2 million women lost their jobs in 1946 as men returned home.
p2: BUT 75% of women said they wanted to keep working regardless.
p3: A sharp contrast to WWI, when most women were happy to return home.

front: How did the GI Bill (1944) reinforce traditional gender roles?
p1: Not explicitly gendered in its wording, but overwhelmingly benefited returning male veterans.
p2: Male education rates rose sharply while women's stagnated.
p3: Reinforced the assumption that men, not women, should be the family's breadwinner.

front: How did Dr Spock's book shape the post-war housewife ideal?
p1: 'The Common-Sense Book of Baby and Child Care' (1946) sold 23 million copies by the 1960s.
p2: Actively encouraged women to embrace a nurturing, stay-at-home motherhood role.
p3: Helped cement the 1950s housewife as suburban America's dominant expectation.

front: Was the 1950s housewife ideal the whole economic reality?
p1: Despite the cultural ideal, women still made up 28% of the workforce by the mid-1950s.
p2: Growth was concentrated in service and clerical jobs — teachers, secretaries, salesclerks.
p3: Showed the housewife ideal was aspirational, not universally lived.

front: How did coverture's legal grip on women begin to erode?
p1: The doctrine had held a married woman's legal identity was subsumed entirely by her husband.
p2: Began genuinely eroding from the early 20th century onward.
p3: Married women gradually gained property rights and real financial independence.

front: How did Betty Friedan and NOW launch second-wave feminism?
p1: Friedan's 'Feminine Mystique' (1963) named 'the problem that has no name' among housewives.
p2: Directly challenged the idealised 1950s domestic role.
p3: Co-founded NOW (1966) to push for equality across education, work and reproductive rights.

front: What did radical feminist protests actually achieve?
p1: 1968 Miss America protest rejected traditional beauty standards symbolically.
p2: 'Burial of True Womanhood' (1968) staged the symbolic death of the domesticity ideal.
p3: Generated real media coverage, even when the message was distorted or mocked.

front: How did the contraceptive Pill (1960) change women's lives?
p1: Gave women unprecedented autonomy over their own reproductive choices.
p2: An estimated 6 million women were using it by 1965.
p3: Paved the way for the wider sexual liberation of the decade.

front: What was the significance of Roe v Wade (1973)?
p1: Legalised abortion nationally under the constitutional right to privacy.
p2: A landmark, hard-won victory for the reproductive rights movement.
p3: BUT became a deeply polarising issue, sparking sustained anti-feminist backlash.

front: How did Phyllis Schlafly defeat the ERA?
p1: Led the Stop ERA campaign, arguing it would erode family structures.
p2: Published 'The Power of the Positive Woman' (1977) as a conservative rallying point.
p3: By 1982, only 35 of the required 38 states had ratified it — the ERA failed.

front: How did feminism's own radical fringe risk alienating support?
p1: Steinem's Ms. Magazine (1972) became a major mainstream feminist platform.
p2: BUT groups like 'The Feminists' called for abolishing marriage entirely.
p3: Such extremes alienated moderates and fuelled the wider backlash.

front: What leadership roles did Black women hold within the Black Power movement?
p1: Elaine Brown became Chairperson of the Black Panther Party itself.
p2: Kathleen Cleaver served as the Party's national spokesperson.
p3: Ericka Huggins helped lead the Party's free breakfast programmes.

front: How did Black Power raise awareness of Black women's 'triple oppression'?
p1: Recognised oppression by race, gender and class as genuinely intersecting.
p2: The Afro became a symbol of Black women's pride, rejecting white beauty standards.
p3: Figures like Fannie Lou Hamer and Angela Davis became widely recognised voices.

front: How did male chauvinism limit women's real power within the Black Panthers?
p1: Women were often relegated to typing, cooking and logistical support regardless of ability.
p2: Expected to be 'revolutionary first, Sister second' — even Angela Davis faced this criticism.
p3: Cleaver noted ideas were often dismissed unless a man proposed them instead.

front: Why did the Nation of Islam reject feminism outright?
p1: Dismissed feminism as fundamentally a 'white woman's issue'.
p2: Rejected birth control on principle.
p3: Criticised women who challenged traditional gender roles within the movement.

front: How far did Black Power actually influence the wider, mainstream women's movement?
p1: Directly inspired the rise of Black feminism and its focus on intersectionality.
p2: Encouraged radical feminists more broadly toward direct-action tactics.
p3: BUT NOW and mainstream feminism stayed largely focused on white, middle-class concerns.

front: What was the political position of women by 1992?
p1: 55% of eligible women voted in 1992, against 49% of men.
p2: 1992's 'Year of the Woman' elected 24 women to the House, 2 to the Senate.
p3: BUT women still held only 5% of the Senate and 11% of the House overall.

front: What was the social position of women by 1992?
p1: The ERA remained unratified, defeated by sustained conservative opposition.
p2: Women graduated high school at higher rates than men — 84% against 78%.
p3: Planned Parenthood v Casey (1992) let states impose new restrictions on abortion access.

front: How had family life changed for women by 1992?
p1: The divorce rate had risen to around 50%.
p2: The average birth rate fell to 2.2 children, the lowest since the 19th century.
p3: About 60% of women were now employed outside the home.

front: What was the economic position of women by 1992?
p1: Women made up about 40% of the entire US workforce.
p2: BUT still earned only around 75% of what men earned for the same work.
p3: Women of colour faced additional barriers on top of this general gap.
